idiom_name: service module: the ES module itself is the facade, exporting one async function per use case
implementation_notes: ES modules are the local idiom: a service module (services/orders.js) imports the fine-grained modules and exports one asynchronous function per use case, so importers see a coarse surface while the fine-grained modules remain unexported and - in a package - unimportable through the exports map. What replaces the classic facade class is the module boundary plus its export list; what still has to be decided by hand is where the unit of work lives, since Node has no container, unless a framework (NestJS, Fastify hooks, Knex/Prisma transactions) owns it. Keep the class form when the facade needs injected collaborators or per-request state, and prefer the module form when the workflow is a pure sequence of calls with no configuration to carry.
pitfalls: Module exports are live bindings: reassigning an exported function later changes every importer and makes tests order-dependent; export const bindings and rebind nothing.
Module-level mutable state (a Map used as cache, a shared client) is a process-wide singleton in a long-lived Node server; per-request state must stay in the request.
Circular imports between the facade module and its collaborators leave one side partially initialised, so a facade may see undefined at import time.
